sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title only: Bishop 2002 (Melbourne PhD, Glottolog 5771, already listed). Minerva bot-blocked live downloads today, the handle still redirects to it); text layer present, no scanned needed. Read §1.4.4, §3.4, §3.7, §3.11, §3.13. Chapter 3 is a first-hand metrical analysis of Kuninjku and Manyallaluk Mayali word stress/accent: left-headed unbounded feet aligned to morpheme left edges (each morpheme = one foot except cohering morphemes), no lexical accent, limited quantity sensitivity, initial stress on mono-morphemic roots, Kuninjku default single accent on the leftmost foot (End Rule Left), MM default accent on the root's foot plus an optional penultimate foot boundary. This confirms the catalog's 'morphological' classification and refines it (dialect-specific default accent; the penultimate target of Evans's Gun-Djeihmi/Kundedjnjenghmi description is derived, not positional). It does not supersede Evans 2003, whose principles Bishop explicitly adapts. line added at Nothing left to acquire. Note: the directory also holds non-search companions downloaded on 9/16 (Bishop 2002 Speech Prosody paper, Bishop & Fletcher 2005 OUP chapter scanned, Mansfield 2022 OSF preprint) that were not items in this search of works with stress in the title and were not re-read.

new_statements.quote: As described in Chapter 1 (§1.4.4), feet are left-headed and unbounded in all dialects of BGW. BGW displays quantity sensitivity only in limited circumstances (see §3.6), and has no lexical accent [...] In BGW, the construction of metrical constituents makes reference to the left edge of the morpheme, which is constrained to align with the left edge of a foot (Evans, 1995; in press). [...] Feet are left-headed and unbounded. The left edge of a morpheme must align with the left edge of a foot; therefore: Each morpheme minimally corresponds to a single foot, with the exception of a set of cohering morphemes, which form a foot together with the preceding morpheme.

new_statements.reading: Stress placement in Bininj Gun-wok is morphologically governed: each morpheme (minus cohering ones) forms one unbounded left-headed foot, so stress falls on morpheme-initial syllables; which foot carries the word's single default pitch accent is dialect-specific (Kuninjku: leftmost foot/word-initial; Manyallaluk Mayali: the root's foot, generally rightmost, with an optional extra penultimate foot), and the 'penultimate' primary stress reported for Gun-Djeihmi/Kundedjnjenghmi is the derived outcome of root-final footing rather than a positional rule. This confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding and refines it with dialect-specific default-accent rules and the quantity-sensitivity/emphatic-accent exceptions.

new_statements.quote: The basic word-stress system involves initial stress on most morphological constituents, though this phonological strength is highly variable in its phonetic realisation. Pitch accent anchoring is the main phonetic indicator of stress, but only a subset of stressed syllables are accented in any given utterance, and the selection of this subset is not directly determined by word structure, such as a predictable right-edge, left-edge, or stem-edge rule. [pp.5-6] ... In polysynthetic verbs, feet are constituted by the verb+TAM base, the Subj+Obj prefix string, and by each of the stem elements that falls in between. [p.9] ... One simple restriction is that word-final syllables are not accentable in polysyllabic words. On the other hand, the right-most, non-final stressed syllable is a common target for accent placement [p.14]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's morphological coding and with the Bishop 2002 statement already held by the project (stress on morpheme-initial syllables, each morpheme an unbounded left-headed foot). Adds: the no-final-accent restriction, the rightmost-non-final tendency, closed-penult weight effect in clash resolution, stem-final lexical/TAM exceptions, and the claim that accent selection is phrase-level and variable rather than a word-level default ('perhaps there is no default', p.17) — a softer position than Bishop's dialect-specific default-accent rules recorded in existing_statements, but on the accent layer, not on word-stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is morphologically assigned: the initial syllable of each morphological constituent of the verb (the pronominal prefix string, each incorporated nominal/adverbial stem, and the verb+TAM base) is stressed, each constituent forming one unbounded foot; monomorphemic words are stressed on their initial syllable. Phonetic prominence is pitch accent (H*) anchored to a subset of these stressed syllables; which stressed syllables get accented is not predictable from word structure (different tokens of the same word differ), though word-final syllables are never accentable in polysyllabic words and the rightmost non-final stressed syllable is a common accent target. Mansfield reads Bishop's morphologically driven foot assignment as a single level of foot structure with only a subset of feet selected for accent (fn.4, p.15).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as primary vs secondary: every morpheme-initial syllable is 'stressed' (an abstract phonological category); prominence differences among them are accentual, selected at phrase level. Stressed but unaccented syllables show no measurable duration/vowel-quality prominence (p.13, citing Bishop 2002a pp.226-233), but unstressed vowels may delete while stressed vowels never do (pp.13-14). Complex verbs typically show a 'hat pattern' with H* on the first and last stressed syllables and no detectable accent on medial morphs (p.11).
new_statements.exceptions: Accent clash between adjacent monosyllabic feet is resolved by de-accenting one foot; with all-open syllables either foot may be de-accented, but a closed penult is consistently accented (p.15, citing Evans 2003: 104); two heavy syllables may tolerate adjacent accents (30)-(31). A few lexical stems/constructions take stem-FINAL accent: certain incorporated nominals, e.g. arri-bu(le-rri) 'we Aboriginal people', and certain TAM allomorphs in certain dialects, e.g. ba-wa(rre-meninj) 'it would go bad' (p.16, citing Evans 2003: 102), with 'no known explanation'. Lexicalised compounds (bo-ngun 'liquid-eat') lack the bimoraic foot minimum that syntactically incorporated roots show (p.14).
new_statements.identity_note: The work treats Bininj Gun-wok as a dialect cluster (Kunwinjku, Mayali, Kune etc.), synthesising Bishop 2002a/b and Evans 2003 rather than reporting new field data; it notes that some stem-final accent exceptions hold for 'certain TAM allomorphs in certain dialects' (p.16). It also draws on Dalabon (dala1237), treated explicitly as a separate language with 'very similar' prosody (p.5, p.19), for comparison; the Ngalakgan and Murrinhpatha sections concern other languages.

sources.quote: The data presented in this chapter demonstrate that the location of pitch accents in BGW words is basically conditioned by metrical structure, which is calculated on the basis of morphological structure within the morphosyntactic word. [...] In Kuninjku, a default single accent typically associates with the head of the leftmost foot in a polypedal phonological word, and a second accent generally associates with the rightmost foot. In Manyallaluk Mayali, a default single accent associates with the root of the morphosyntactic word, however, again, a second accent seeks out a word-peripheral foot: the leftmost foot.
sources.note: Primarily an intonation thesis, but Chapter 3 (pp.111-211) is a full first-hand metrical analysis of word stress/accent in the Kuninjku and Manyallaluk Mayali (MM) dialects. sources.quote: '[BGW] has conventionally been described as a stress language (Evans 1995; Fletcher and Evans 2000) with no lexical use of pitch. Its polysynthetic structure results in complex metrical stress rules (see Evans (1995, 2003) and Bishop (2001, 2003: ch. 3) for a more detailed treatment than can be given here). Pitch accents can anchor to more than one metrically strong syllable within the word: a single morphosyntactic word may carry two to three pitch accents.'
sources.note: Cross-dialect intonation survey (six dialects incl. Manyallaluk Mayali, which Evans says does not follow his rules); defers to Evans 2003/Bishop 2002 ch.3 for the stress rules.
